Q5. Can a face presentation deliver vaginally?

blocks.text: Yes, selected cases can, particularly when the mentum is anterior, provided there is adequate pelvic capacity, satisfactory progress and reassuring maternal and fetal condition.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. What if the mentum is persistently posterior?

blocks.text: Vaginal delivery is generally not possible because the extended fetal head cannot complete the required mechanism of birth, so Caesarean birth is usually required.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What is the difference between face and brow presentation?

blocks.text: In face presentation the head is fully hyperextended and the face presents. In brow presentation the head is partially extended and the forehead presents.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What can happen to a brow presentation?

blocks.text: It may convert to vertex if flexion occurs or to face if extension increases. Persistent brow presentation is usually obstructed and generally requires Caesarean birth.

blocks.text: **Q10. What would you do if a woman with transverse lie suddenly reports that her waters have broken?**

I would arrange urgent assessment, assess maternal and fetal wellbeing, confirm presentation, perform appropriate fetal monitoring, assess for cord prolapse and involve senior obstetric staff. If persistent transverse lie is present in labour, Caesarean birth is generally required.

**“How would you approach a malpresentation or malposition?”**

“I would first assess the maternal and fetal condition and establish the gestational age and stage of labour. I would perform abdominal palpation to determine lie, presentation, position and engagement, followed by fetal heart assessment. If indicated, I would perform a carefully consented vaginal examination to identify the presenting part, position, station, cervical dilatation, caput and moulding. I would confirm the diagnosis with ultrasound where necessary and assess labour progress and fetal wellbeing. Management depends on the specific abnormality: some malpositions such as OP may rotate spontaneously, whereas persistent transverse lie, persistent brow or unfavourable face presentation may require Caesarean birth. I would also specifically assess for cord prolapse, obstructed labour and fetal compromise.”
